questions.question: Explain what a fixed asset register contains, its control relationship with the general ledger, and the three uses it serves.
questions.expected_answer: One page per asset carrying its description and identifying detail (registration or serial number), purchase date and supplier, cost price, depreciation method and rate, then year by year the annual depreciation, accumulated depreciation and carrying value, plus location and the responsible person — closed off on disposal with the date, proceeds and profit or loss. The register is the detail behind the ledger's class totals, exactly as the debtors' list stands behind Debtors Control: the sum of all pages' costs must equal the asset account, and the sum of accumulated depreciation must equal that account, with any difference investigated as a standing control. Its three uses: control (assets can be produced on inspection, so theft and unrecorded disposals surface), decisions (age, remaining value and history inform replace-or-repair), and audit (every statement figure traces to a page, a rate and a calculation).

questions.question: Assemble the cost of a fixed asset, distinguish capital from revenue expenditure, and state the consequences of misclassifying each way.
questions.expected_answer: Cost includes everything necessary to bring the asset into use: purchase price, delivery, installation and any initial modification — so a machine invoiced at R120 000 with R5 500 delivery and R9 500 installation enters at R135 000, and all future depreciation computes on that figure. A registered vendor excludes VAT, which is claimed as input tax. Capital expenditure extends the asset's life or capacity beyond its original condition and is added to cost; revenue expenditure maintains the existing standard and is an expense of the year. Treating capital as revenue understates profit, the asset and future depreciation; treating revenue as capital overstates profit and the asset and depreciates money that bought nothing lasting — the error that flatters results, which is why auditors sample large repair invoices in both directions.

questions.question: Calculate three years of depreciation on a R320 000 vehicle bought 1 June at 15% on the diminishing balance (year end 28 February), and explain the treatment of a fully depreciated asset.
questions.expected_answer: Year one: a full year would be 15% of R320 000 = R48 000, but the vehicle was owned nine months (June to February), so R48 000 × 9/12 = R36 000; carrying value R284 000. Year two, a full year: 15% of R284 000 = R42 600; carrying value R241 400. Year three: 15% of R241 400 = R36 210. Each figure is entered on the register page beside the accumulated total and carrying value. Slicing happens only in the year an asset arrives or leaves. A fully depreciated asset has no further charge — you may not depreciate below zero, since the business cannot consume more than the asset cost — and a nominal R1 is often left so an asset still in use does not vanish from the records. It remains on the register, under control and producible on inspection.
